body.statement: For every \((p,k,m,M,s,V)\in\mathfrak T\) and every \(P\in\mathcal M_{p,k}(m,M,s,V)\), \(F\) is normalized, nonnegative, and monotone, and \[\gamma_k(F)\ge\Gamma=\frac{m}{M}\frac{s}{V}=\frac{1}{KR}.\] The bound is independent of \(p\) and \(k\).
body.justification: This is the central achievability theorem: sparse covariance conditioning and residual signal-to-noise margins alone certify a nonvanishing approximation ratio.
body.gap: Lin et al. leave variable selection open, while Das and Kempe control a one-response regression objective; neither supplies the extra residual-scale factor or the causal transport comparison.
body.consumer: Investigators facing a hard baseline-measurement budget obtain an ex ante certificate for forward selection without dependence on the number of available covariates.
body.proof_tex:
Normalization follows immediately from the gain definition: \(F(\varnothing)=0\).  We first verify monotonicity without imposing a hidden residual-positivity condition outside the budget range.  For arbitrary \(L\subseteq S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\), let \(T=S\setminus L\), let \(H\) and \(d_a\) be the corresponding Schur-complement quantities, and put \(q_a=H^{-1/2}d_a\).  The block residual identity gives
\(r_a(S)=r_a(L)-\|q_a\|_2^2\geq0\).  The endpoint algebra used in \(\texttt{lem:angular-identity}\), which remains valid when a residual is zero, gives
\[
 B(S)-B(L)=2\left\{\sqrt{r_0(L)r_1(L)}
 -q_0^{\mathsf T}q_1-\sqrt{r_0(S)r_1(S)}\right\}.
\]
The vectors \((q_a^{\mathsf T},\sqrt{r_a(S)})^{\mathsf T}\) have norms \(\sqrt{r_a(L)}\).  Cauchy--Schwarz therefore makes the expression in braces nonnegative.  Thus \(B\), and hence \(F\), is monotone; normalization then implies \(F(S)\geq0\).

It remains to prove the ratio bound.  Fix an eligible disjoint pair \(L,T\) with \(\Delta(L,T)>0\), and abbreviate \(r_a=r_a(L)\), \(D=\operatorname{diag}(H)\), and
\[
 w_j=\frac{H^{1/2}e_j}{\sqrt{H_{jj}}},\qquad j\in T.
\]
Each \(w_j\) is a unit vector and, by \(\texttt{lem:angular-identity}\),
\[
 \sum_{j\in T}w_jw_j^{\mathsf T}
 =H^{1/2}D^{-1}H^{1/2}\succeq(m/M)I.
\]
The normalized singleton residual score is exactly
\[
 \frac{d_{a,j}}{\sqrt{H_{jj}}\sqrt{r_a}}=w_j^{\mathsf T}u_a;
\]
this equality is the step that retains coordinate meaning after joint whitening.

We use the following elementary hemisphere comparison.  If
\(\|u\|_2,\|v\|_2\leq\sqrt{1-q}\) with \(0<q\leq1\), then
\[
 \frac12\|u-v\|_2^2\leq g(u,v)
 \leq\frac{1}{2q}\|u-v\|_2^2.
\]
The lower inequality is obtained by discarding the final nonnegative square in
\(2g(u,v)=\|u-v\|_2^2+\{\sqrt{1-\|u\|_2^2}-\sqrt{1-\|v\|_2^2}\}^2\).
For the upper inequality, the gradient of \(x\mapsto\sqrt{1-\|x\|_2^2}\) on the convex ball of radius \(\sqrt{1-q}\) has norm at most \(\sqrt{(1-q)/q}\).  Integration along the line segment from \(u\) to \(v\) bounds the last square by \((1-q)\|u-v\|_2^2/q\).  The case \(q=1\) is immediate.

Apply this comparison with \(q=s/V\), which is permitted by the radius conclusion of \(\texttt{lem:angular-identity}\), and put \(\delta=u_0-u_1\).  The singleton angular identities, the lower hemisphere inequality, and the frame bound give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{j\in T}\Delta(L,\{j\})
 &=2\sqrt{r_0r_1}\sum_{j\in T}
   g(w_j^{\mathsf T}u_0,w_j^{\mathsf T}u_1)\\
 &\geq\sqrt{r_0r_1}\sum_{j\in T}(w_j^{\mathsf T}\delta)^2\\
 &\geq\sqrt{r_0r_1}(m/M)\|\delta\|_2^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The joint angular identity and the upper hemisphere inequality give
\[
 \Delta(L,T)\leq\sqrt{r_0r_1}(V/s)\|\delta\|_2^2.
\]
Positivity of \(\Delta(L,T)\) forces \(\delta\neq0\), so division is legitimate and yields
\[
 \frac{\sum_{j\in T}\Delta(L,\{j\})}{\Delta(L,T)}
 \geq\frac{m}{M}\frac{s}{V}=\Gamma=\frac1{KR}.
\]
Taking the infimum and applying the cap at one in the definition of \(\gamma_k\) proves the claim, since \(0<\Gamma\leq1\).  Neither the comparison nor its constants depend on \(p\) or \(k\).
